pharm: Long-acting oral diphenylbutylpiperidine antipsychotic; a potent dopamine D2 antagonist whose very long duration of action allows once-weekly oral dosing.
quick: Use only if clearly needed; neonatal EPS/withdrawal risk
Extrapyramidal symptoms, ECG/QTc, prolactin, metabolic parameters
summary: Penfluridol is a long-acting oral typical antipsychotic of the diphenylbutylpiperidine class used for maintenance treatment of chronic schizophrenia. Its distinctive feature is once-weekly oral dosing, which aids adherence and bridges daily oral therapy and injectable depots. It is a dopamine D2 antagonist with a high risk of extrapyramidal symptoms. It is not FDA-approved or marketed in the US; the data here are drawn from regional sources and a Cochrane review.
indications: Chronic psychotic disorders, particularly in patients who are non-adherent with daily oral therapy or do not tolerate injectable depots

dosage.n: Higher doses increase EPS without added benefit; reported range 5-160 mg/week

admin: Take by mouth once every 7 days on the same day each week
May be taken with or without food
Emphasize to the patient that this is NOT a daily medication - daily dosing risks serious overdose given the long half-life
Effects persist for many days after each dose
moa: Penfluridol antagonizes central postsynaptic dopamine D2 receptors (with affinity also at D1, D3, D5 and some serotonergic receptors and T-type calcium channels). Its high lipophilicity and very long terminal half-life produce a prolonged antipsychotic effect allowing once-weekly dosing.

absolute: Pre-existing CNS depression or coma of any cause
Hypersensitivity to penfluridol or other diphenylbutylpiperidines
relative: Cardiac disease or QT prolongation risk

preg: No formal modern pregnancy category is assigned; use only if clearly needed. Third-trimester exposure may cause neonatal extrapyramidal symptoms and withdrawal (a class effect), and the long half-life means persistent fetal exposure.
lact: Excretion in human milk is unknown; use with caution.
renal: Use with caution in severe renal impairment; no quantitative dosing scheme is defined.
hepatic: Use with caution and consider dose reduction because the drug is hepatically metabolized; some regional references list hepatic impairment as a major precaution or contraindication.

major: CNS depressants, alcohol, and opioids - additive CNS depression
QT-prolonging drugs - increased risk of torsades de pointes
Levodopa and dopamine agonists - mutual antagonism
Other antipsychotics - increased EPS and neuroleptic malignant syndrome risk
interactions.food: No clinically significant interaction (peak at ~2 hours)

common: Extrapyramidal symptoms (akathisia, parkinsonism, dyskinesia, tremor, rigidity)
emergency: Torsades de pointes / sudden cardiac death

monitoring: Extrapyramidal symptoms and abnormal involuntary movements at each visit
Baseline and periodic ECG/QTc and electrolytes (potassium, magnesium, calcium)
Liver function and complete blood count; watch for neuroleptic malignant syndrome
counsel: Take this medicine ONCE A WEEK on the same day - it is NOT a daily tablet
It can cause drowsiness or dizziness - take care when driving and rise slowly from sitting/lying
Report muscle stiffness, tremor, restlessness, abnormal movements, high fever with rigidity, fainting, or irregular heartbeat
Do not stop abruptly; the effect lasts for several days after each dose
pk: Plasma peak ~2 hours after a dose
~66 hours overall (biphasic; terminal up to ~120 hours / ~5 days)
Room temperature, protected from light and moisture
pearls: Not FDA-approved or marketed in the US - data here are from regional sources and a Cochrane review
A unique long-acting ORAL antipsychotic that bridges daily oral therapy and injectable depots
Once-weekly dosing aids adherence; Cochrane data show better retention than depots and efficacy comparable to other typical antipsychotics
Only mildly sedating but prone to extrapyramidal symptoms
Long half-life means toxicity and effects persist for many days - never escalate to daily dosing
missed: Take the missed weekly dose when you remember; if it is close to the next scheduled weekly dose, skip it - do NOT double the dose (toxicity risk given the long half-life). Contact the prescriber if several doses are missed.
overdose: There is no specific antidote; management is supportive. Provide airway/breathing/circulation support with continuous cardiac monitoring and a 12-lead ECG. Treat hypotension with IV fluids then norepinephrine (avoid pure beta-agonists), severe dystonia with anticholinergics (benztropine) or benzodiazepines, and neuroleptic malignant syndrome with cooling and dantrolene/bromocriptine. Monitor for a prolonged period because toxicity persists for days.
